title: Against your will (Avot 4:22)
hook: against your will you were born, you live and you die, and still you give account
tomorrow: why would God need ten sayings to make one world?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two pages: new paper and erased paper. Both still write. Today the last saying of chapter four asks what the page was never asked.

Every app makes you scroll the terms and tap agree. Life skipped that step. Nobody signed off on their birthday, their family, their hometown, the face in the mirror. So if you were never asked, why would you still have to answer? Avot asks exactly that, in one strange breath. It says against your will, over and over, and then, in the same sentence, that you'll give account.
screen: `NO TERMS, NO AGREE BUTTON.` → `NEVER ASKED.` → `THEN WHY ANSWER?`

segments.voice: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar closes chapter four with a heavy saying. Those born will die; the dead will live again; the living will be judged. Before God there's no wrong, no forgetting, no favoritism, no bribe. Don't let your inclination promise you the grave is a place to hide. Then the refrain. Against your will you were formed. Against your will you were born. Against your will you live. Against your will you die. And against your will you'll give account before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. Here's the puzzle: if so much was never your choice, how is the account fair? Look at what's on the list. Being formed, being born, being alive, dying. That's the frame, and nobody picks the frame. What's not on the list is everything you did inside it. The account isn't for being born. It's for what you did with the life you were handed. A midrash pictures the soul itself not wanting to go into the world, and sent anyway. The mishnah doesn't argue. It just sets two things side by side: given, and still accountable. Some readers hear it as stern. Others hear fairness: an honest account, with nothing forgotten and nobody bought off. You didn't choose the stage. The lines you say on it are yours.
screen: `ELAZAR HAKAPPAR CLOSES CHAPTER FOUR.` · `AGAINST YOUR WILL, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THE FRAME IS GIVEN.` · `THE LINES ARE YOURS.` · then, large: `GIVEN, AND STILL ACCOUNTABLE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up and open. One at a time, set into them the things you didn't choose: the family you were born into, the body you live in, the place you started. Don't argue with any of them. For the last few breaths, let your fingers curl gently, the way you'd hold something handed to you.
screen: `PALMS UP.` · `WHAT YOU DIDN'T CHOOSE.` · `HOLD WHAT WAS HANDED TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Against your will: Elazar HaKappar's refrain for what nobody chooses. Being born, living, dying. And then, still, the account.
Hold on to this one: given, and still accountable, the stage and then the lines. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Jewish custom Pirkei Avot is read on summer Shabbat afternoons, a chapter a week; chapter four ends with Elazar HaKappar's saying, and the reader goes on to chapter five.

original.note: Hebrew: against your will, the refrain of Avot 4:22.

trapdoor: what you thought: if it wasn't my choice, it isn't on me.
what it means: birth, life and death are the frame; the account is for what you did inside it.
what a scholar hears: the refrain follows a warning not to treat the grave as a refuge; a midrash in Tanchuma pictures the soul sent into the world unwilling.

a vow you were pressured into keeping
a punishment for breaking God's law
